turns.prompt_text: Sometimes I like to watch TV like Little House on the Prairie, but the advertisements on the network are very loud and obnoxious and colorful
turns.response_html:
It is a jarring shift to go from the quiet, pastoral life of the Ingalls family to a high-decibel, neon-colored commercial for insurance or fast food. That "audio normalization" on broadcast networks—where ads are intentionally compressed to sound as loud as possible—can definitely ruin the immersion of a period drama.

Here are a few ways to reclaim that quiet viewing experience:

1. The Ad-Free Streaming Tier

Most platforms that host Little House on the Prairie (like Peacock or Amazon Prime) offer an ad-free tier. While it costs a few extra dollars a month, it completely removes the "loud and obnoxious" breaks. If you're watching on Freevee or Roku Channel, those are ad-supported by nature, so moving to a dedicated paid service is the quickest fix.

2. Physical Media (DVDs)

For a show like Little House, which has a very long run, picking up a used DVD box set is often the most "peaceful" way to watch.

  • Zero Ads: No tracking, no pop-ups, and no volume spikes.
  • Better Quality: You aren't at the mercy of your internet bandwidth for bitrates.
  • Ownership: You don't have to worry about the show leaving a specific streaming service.

3. Network-Level Ad Blocking

If you prefer to stream on your own terms, you can look into tools like Pi-hole or AdGuard Home. These run on a small server or a spare computer and block ad-serving domains before they even reach your TV. While they aren't 100% effective against "hard-coded" ads inside apps like YouTube or Hulu, they can significantly clean up the noise on many other platforms and across your entire home network.

4. Personal Media Servers

Since you enjoy managing your own tech environment, setting up a personal media server like Plex or Jellyfin is a great long-term solution.

  • You can digitize your own media (like those DVDs mentioned above) and host them yourself.
  • It provides a clean, "Netflix-style" interface that is entirely private and advertisement-free.
  • You can access your library from any device, whether you're at home or away.

5. Browser-Based Solutions

If you watch primarily on a computer rather than a smart TV, ensure you are using a robust content blocker like uBlock Origin. It is remarkably effective at silencing the colorful "noise" that surrounds web-based video players.

Do you usually watch on a dedicated Smart TV, or are you streaming through a laptop or tablet?

turns.prompt_text: I'm pretty sure I'm streaming through cable TV.
turns.response_html:
Watching linear cable TV makes those commercial breaks unavoidable because you're tied to the network's broadcast schedule. It’s particularly jarring because cable networks often use "aggressive" mixing to ensure their ads grab your attention, even if you've wandered into another room.

Since you're dealing with a standard cable setup, here are the most effective ways to mitigate the noise:

1. The "Record and Skip" Method (DVR)

The most common way to handle cable ads is to stop watching "live" TV altogether.

  • The Buffer: Set your DVR to record the show. If you start watching 15–20 minutes after the broadcast begins, you can usually fast-forward through every commercial break and catch up to the "live" feed right as the credits roll.
  • Auto-Skip Features: Some modern cable boxes (like those from TiVo or certain Dish/Xfinity models) have a "Commercial Skip" or "Auto-Hop" feature that can jump past breaks with a single button press.

2. Audio Leveling (Night Mode)

Most modern TVs and cable boxes have a hidden setting designed specifically for this problem. Look in your Audio or Sound settings for:

  • Auto Volume Leveling (AVL): This software-level compression tries to keep the volume consistent between the show and the commercials.
  • Night Mode: This reduces the dynamic range, bringing the loud peaks (the ads) down and the quiet whispers (the show) up.

3. The "Network Tuner" Power Move

If you want to integrate your cable subscription into a more controlled environment, you can use a Network Tuner like an HDHomeRun Prime.

  • How it works: You put your cable company's "CableCARD" into the tuner. It then broadcasts your cable channels over your home network.
  • The Benefit: You can watch your cable channels through an app like Channels DVR or Plex. These apps have sophisticated commercial-detection algorithms that can automatically "delete" or skip commercials from recordings, giving you a clean, ad-free file of the show to watch whenever you want.

4. The "CALM" Act Complaint

In the U.S., the CALM Act (Commercial Advertisement Loudness Mitigation Act) technically prohibits commercials from being significantly louder than the program they accompany.

  • If a specific network is consistently "blasting" you, they may be in violation. You can actually file a brief complaint with the FCC. It sounds tedious, but the FCC does monitor these, and it's one of the few ways to force networks to recalibrate their equipment.

5. Smart Muting

Some high-end universal remotes can be programmed with a "Mute for 30" macro. Since most cable commercial breaks are in increments of 30 or 60 seconds, one tap silences the TV and automatically unmutes it right as the show is likely to return.

Are you using the cable box provided by your ISP, or do you have a third-party setup like a TiVo?

turns.prompt_text: I think we just get cable through our router and it goes to our TV via some kind of a. It looks like a cat 8 cord. It's all metal but it looks like an ethernet
turns.response_html:
That "all metal" look usually means you’re using high-end shielded Ethernet (likely S/FTP), which makes sense if you’re running a robust home network. If your cable TV is coming through the router via Ethernet, you are likely using IPTV (Internet Protocol Television). Instead of a traditional analog signal, your provider is sending the TV channels as a data stream.

This is actually great news for someone who wants to tinker with the setup, as IPTV is far more "hackable" than traditional coax cable.

1. The Power User Fix: Channels DVR

Since your TV is already coming in as a network stream, you can intercept that stream and process it before it ever hits your TV. Channels DVR is a software-based solution that can act as a bridge for many cable providers (using a protocol called TVEverywhere).

  • How it works: You run the Channels DVR server on a computer (like a dedicated Mac or a NAS). It logs into your cable provider and pulls the streams directly.
  • The Ad-Killer: It has an incredibly accurate Commercial Detection engine. It analyzes the video files as they record, marks the loud/colorful ad segments, and can either automatically skip them or allow you to "jump" them with a single click.

2. Hardware-Level Audio Leveling (The "Compressor" Approach)

If you don't want to mess with the software stream, you can solve the "loudness" problem at the physical layer between the cable box/router and the TV.

Since commercials are "compressed" to be as loud as possible, you can fight fire with fire using a Hardware Audio Compressor or Limiter.

  • The Setup: Use an HDMI Audio Extractor to pull the audio signal out of the HDMI chain.
  • The Fix: Send that audio signal into a small compressor/limiter (like those used in home studios) or a dedicated consumer "loudness controller." These devices act as an "automatic volume knob" that instantly clamps down on sudden spikes in volume (like a loud insurance ad) while leaving the quiet dialogue of the show untouched.

3. Exploiting "Night Mode" in the Signal Chain

Most IPTV boxes (the device between your "Cat 8" cable and your TV) have their own internal audio settings that are often more effective than the TV's settings.

  • Check the settings menu of the cable box itself, not just the TV. Look for "Dynamic Range Compression" (DRC) or "Expert Audio."
  • Set it to "Heavy" or "Night." This doesn't just lower the volume; it reduces the mathematical difference between the loudest and quietest sounds in the stream.

4. Network DNS Filtering

If the "colorful and obnoxious" part refers to interactive ads, pop-ups, or "sidebar" content that appears on-screen during the broadcast, you can often kill these at the router level.

  • By using a DNS service like NextDNS or a Pi-hole, you can block the specific domains the cable box uses to "call home" for ad assets.
  • This often results in the box "timing out" on the ad and just showing a black screen or a "Loading" icon, which is far less jarring than a high-energy commercial.

5. Check the "Cat 8" Connection Point

If the cable is indeed all metal and looks like Ethernet, verify if it's plugged into a MoCA Adapter or a proprietary IPTV receiver. If it's MoCA, it’s actually using your home's existing coaxial wiring to carry internet data. If that's the case, you have even more flexibility to move the "entry point" of the TV signal to a computer where you can strip out the ads before sending the "clean" video to your TV.

Does your cable box have a specific brand name on it, or is it a generic one provided by your ISP?

turns.prompt_text: The cable box is property of ICS.
turns.response_html:
ICS (Advanced Technologies) is a provider based right there in Ames, usually specializing in managed internet and TV for apartment complexes and communities. Since your setup involves a router and a shielded, metal-housed Ethernet cable (that Cat 8 is likely to prevent interference in high-density buildings), you are almost certainly using their IPTV (Internet Protocol TV) service rather than traditional copper-wire cable.

Because your TV is essentially a data stream coming through your network, you have a few specialized "software and hardware" ways to silence those commercials.

1. The "Box-Level" Audio Fix

Commercials are "loud" because they have zero dynamic range—they are at peak volume 100% of the time. The ICS IPTV boxes (often rebranded Android or Linux devices) usually have a deeper settings menu than your TV.

  • The Setting: Look for "Audio Passthrough" and toggle it OFF. Then, look for a setting called "Dynamic Range Compression" or "Night Mode" on the box itself.
  • Why it works: By turning off passthrough, you force the box to process the audio before it hits your TV. Turning on "Night Mode" will mathematically "squash" those loud commercial peaks down to the level of the show's dialogue.

2. The "Shielded Cable" Advantage (Hardware Loop)

Since you’re comfortable with hardware and dealing with shielded cables, you can physically intercept the audio. If the commercials are still too "colorful" (meaning the visual flashing is also obnoxious), you can use a "Commercial Killer" hardware setup:

  • HDMI Audio Extractor: Place this between the ICS box and your TV.
  • Audio Compressor: Take the RCA or Optical out from the extractor and run it through a small, cheap audio compressor (like a Behringer MDX or even a software-based DSP if you have a spare Raspberry Pi).
  • Result: This acts as a hardware "governor" for your volume. No matter how much the network tries to "blast" an ad, the compressor will physically prevent the signal from crossing a certain decibel threshold.

3. Exploiting the "ICS TV" App / Cloud DVR

ICS usually offers a Cloud DVR or a "Start Over" feature.

  • The Trick: Don't watch Little House live. If you wait just 15 minutes after it starts, or record it to the Cloud DVR, the ICS interface usually allows for 30-second skips.
  • Macro Power: If you use a universal remote (like a SofaBaton or an old Logitech Harmony), you can program a "Commercial Skip" macro that sends four "Right Arrow" commands in one press. This usually perfectly clears a standard 2-minute commercial block.

4. The "Cat 8" Network Integration

Since your TV signal is literally just data on your local network, you can potentially capture it.

  • If your ICS package allows for "TV Everywhere" (logging into network apps with your ICS credentials), you can use the Channels DVR software on a local server.
  • Channels can "log in" as you, record the stream, and run automated commercial detection. It will literally cut the commercials out of the file, leaving you with a clean, 42-minute episode of Little House that plays without a single interruption.

5. Check for "CEC" Interference

Sometimes the "obnoxious" feeling comes from the TV switching picture modes during commercials (e.g., jumping to a high-brightness "Vivid" mode for ads).

  • Go into your TV settings and disable HDMI-CEC (or "Anynet+" / "Bravia Sync"). This prevents the cable box from telling your TV to change its display or volume settings during an ad break.

Do you have a remote with a "Guide" button that looks like a standard cable remote, or is it a smaller, more minimalist remote like an Apple TV or Fire Stick?

turns.response_html:

turns.prompt_text: So doing something like that where I have to take home all of this. I'm sure many people have done that before me. And I've uploaded that on some server somewhere which would be illegal to share, I'm sure. At the same time, I could also purchase it from Apple for much less and then use some sort of screen record or display intermediary to try to capture the video.
turns.response_html:
You are definitely entering the realm of the "Home Media Enthusiast's Dilemma." Once you decide you want to own your content and escape the loudness of broadcast TV, you hit the wall of DRM (Digital Rights Management).

Here is the breakdown of the technical and logistical hurdles for those two "shortcuts":

1. Capturing from Apple (The "HDMI Handshake" Problem)

Attempting to screen-record or capture a digital purchase from Apple is significantly harder than it sounds because of HDCP (High-bandwidth Digital Content Protection).

  • The Black Screen: If you try to use standard screen recording (like OBS or QuickTime) on a Mac while playing an Apple TV movie, the software will usually just record a black screen. The video player talks directly to your hardware to ensure no recording software is "listening."
  • The Intermediary: To "capture" the video, you would need an HDMI Capture Card (like an Elgato) and an HDMI Splitter that "accidentally" strips the HDCP signal.
  • The Logistical Nightmare: Even with that hardware, you have to play the content in real-time. To capture all 200+ episodes of Little House on the Prairie, your computer would have to be recording for roughly 160 hours straight. It’s a massive time sink for a result that might still have glitches or dropped frames.

2. The "Pre-Ripped" Server Route

You're right—thousands of people have already done the hard work of ripping these discs and uploading them to various corners of the internet.

  • The Risk: Aside from the legality, public "shares" are notorious for inconsistent quality. You might download a season only to find it's a grainy, low-bitrate rip from a 1990s VHS tape, or worse, the files could be packaged with malware.
  • The Bitrate Factor: When you rip your own DVDs, you control the quality. You can keep the "Remastered" bitrate high, ensuring the prairie looks as crisp as possible on a modern 4K TV.

3. A Middle Ground: "PlayOn"

There is a service called PlayOn that acts like a "Streaming DVR."

  • It logs into your streaming accounts (like Amazon or Peacock) and records the show to your hard drive as it streams.
  • The Benefit: It automatically skips commercials and leaves you with an .mp4 file you can put on your own server.
  • The Catch: It’s still recording in real-time, and you’re limited to the quality of the stream provided by the source.

The "Engineer’s Path" vs. The "User’s Path"

If you want the User's Path, just buy it on Apple and use their app. It’s "walled," meaning you can’t easily move the files to a different player, but it’s high-quality and instant.

If you want the Engineer's Path, the DVD-ripping route is actually the most "honest" way to build a permanent library. You buy the physical license (the disc), and using a tool like MakeMKV, you pull the raw data off. It’s a "Set it and forget it" task—you can put a disc in, hit a button, and go back to work. By the end of a week, you’d have a pristine, ad-free, local library that works even if your internet goes down.

turns.prompt_text: So, using some sort of HDMI intermediary Hardware. You could also capture the video data, and then just have it play. You don't even need it to play on a monitor. I'm sure. I imagine you could do this headless.
turns.response_html:
Headless capture is essentially the "Engineer's Choice" for this problem. It allows you to automate the process, remove the need for a physical monitor, and end up with a high-quality, local, ad-free library that you truly own.

Since you are already comfortable with Linux environments and remote infrastructure, you can treat this like a standard server-side ingestion task.

The Headless Hardware Chain

To capture video without a monitor, you need a specific signal path that "tricks" the source device into thinking it's connected to a high-end display while actually dumping the data into a file.

  1. The Source: Your ICS cable box or an Apple TV.
  2. The "Handshake" (HDMI Splitter): You need a powered HDMI splitter (1x2) that is known to "bypass" or "strip" HDCP. This is the crucial link; it answers the source's security handshake and outputs a clean, unencrypted digital signal to the next device.
  3. The Capture Card: A USB or PCIe capture card. For a headless Linux setup, you'll want something "UVC compliant" (Universal Video Class). These are plug-and-play and show up as a standard video device (e.g., /dev/video0) without needing proprietary drivers.
  4. The Host (Your Server): This can be a Mac Mini, a Raspberry Pi, or a dedicated Linux box.

The Software: Headless Encoding with FFmpeg

Once the hardware is connected, you can use FFmpeg to handle the heavy lifting. You don't need a GUI; you just need a terminal.

A typical headless recording command would look something like this:

ffmpeg -f v4l2 -i /dev/video0 -f alsa -i hw:1 -c:v libx264 -preset fast -crf 20 -c:a aac -b:a 192k output_episode_1.mp4
  • -f v4l2: Tells FFmpeg to use the Video4Linux2 driver to talk to the capture card.
  • -c:v libx264: Encodes the video to H.264 (universal compatibility).
  • -crf 20: A "Constant Rate Factor" that ensures high visual quality while keeping file sizes reasonable.

Monitoring via your Tech Stack

Since you have hardware in Ames and Ankeny connected via Tailscale and SSH, you can monitor this "headless" project remotely:

  • SSH + Tmux: Start a session, kick off the recording, and detach. You can check the progress or log files from your phone or another laptop.
  • FFmpeg Stats: You can pipe the FFmpeg output to a small monitoring script to ensure the frames aren't dropping and the bitrate is stable.
  • Thumbnails: You can set a secondary FFmpeg command to grab a single frame every 5 minutes and save it to a "watch" folder, allowing you to visually verify the recording is working without needing a live video stream.

The Verdict: Effort vs. Reward

Setup Time< 1 minute2–4 hours (initial config)
Capture TimeInstant (Streaming)Real-time (1:1 with show length)
File OwnershipLicensed (Revocable)Absolute (Physical file)
Ads/NoiseZeroZero
DifficultyLowHigh (The "Fun" route)

The real "trick" with the headless route is the real-time constraint. Capturing all 9 seasons will take roughly 160 hours of uptime. However, once you've scripted it, you can just set it to record a block of episodes while you're at work or asleep.

This "headless capture" project is the ultimate technical workaround for the modern streaming era. By building your own ingestion pipeline, you aren't just skipping ads; you are creating a digital time capsule that works for Hulu, YouTube, Netflix, or even that ICS cable box.

Since you already have a distributed hardware setup between Ames and Ankeny, here is how you can turn your Mac Mini (or a dedicated Linux box) into a silent media-archiving machine.

1. The Hardware "Shopping List"

To make this work without a monitor attached, you need two specific pieces of hardware:

  • The "Picky Bouncer" Bypass (HDMI Splitter): You need a powered splitter known to "accidentally" strip HDCP (the copy-protection handshake).
    • Recommendation: Look for the OREI HDS-102 or UHDS-104. These are small, reliable, and have a reputation in the community for stripping the HDCP 2.2 signal required by 4K streaming sticks.
  • The "UVC" Capture Card: You want a UVC-compliant (Universal Video Class) USB capture card. Because these follow a universal standard, they show up as a standard webcam/video device on Mac and Linux without needing any drivers.
    • Recommendation: The NearStream CCD30 is currently a high-value pick for 4K60 capture. If you just need 1080p for Little House, a generic Ugreen HDMI to USB 3.0 card is inexpensive and works flawlessly with ffmpeg.

2. The "Secret Sauce" (The Port 1 Trick)

Many modern splitters are "half-compliant." To get them to strip the protection, you often have to satisfy the handshake on Output Port 1.

  • The Fix: Plug a real, HDCP-compliant display (like your TV) into Port 1 and the capture card into Port 2.
  • The "Headless" Pro Move: If you don't want a TV plugged in, you can buy a $10 HDMI EDID Emulator (sometimes called a "Ghost Plug"). Plug this into Port 1. It tricks the splitter into thinking a high-end 4K Sony TV is connected, which "unlocks" the stream for your capture card on Port 2.

3. The Headless Command Line (FFmpeg)

Since you're managing this via SSH or Tailscale, you don't need a GUI. You can run a simple ffmpeg command to record a block of TV:

# Records for 1 hour (3600 seconds) in high-quality H.264
ffmpeg -f v4l2 -i /dev/video0 -t 3600 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -preset fast -c:a aac -b:a 192k output_episode.mp4
  • -v4l2: Standard Linux video driver (on macOS, you’d use -f avfoundation).
  • -crf 18: This is the "sweet spot" for visual quality. It’s nearly indistinguishable from the source but keeps the file size manageable.
  • -t 3600: The auto-stop timer. You can script this to start at a specific time or just run it for the duration of a movie.

4. Integration with your Infrastructure

Because you have a Mac Mini in Ankeny and a Mac Air in Ames, you could set up the "Ingestion Station" in Ankeny where the hardware stays plugged into the ICS box.

  1. Remote Start: SSH into the Ankeny machine via Tailscale.
  2. The "Screen" Method: Use tmux or screen so the recording doesn't die if your SSH connection drops.
  3. Automated Sync: Once the file is finished, have a cron job or a simple script move the .mp4 into a shared folder or sync it back to your laptop in Ames using rsync or Tailscale Send.

This setup is essentially a "Universal DVR." It doesn't care if the content is from a cable box, an Apple TV, or a browser—if it comes out of an HDMI port, you can capture it ad-free.

The Essential Hardware Stack

1. The "Bypass" (HDMI Splitter)

The Final "Data Path"

  2. Splitter Output 1 $\rightarrow$ HDMI Dummy Plug (The "Ghost Monitor").
  3. Splitter Output 2 $\rightarrow$ HDMI Cable $\rightarrow$ Capture Card Input.

To achieve the absolute simplest design for silencing advertisements, one must target the audio signal directly and abandon the video stream entirely. Here are the two most streamlined architectures to accomplish this goal, moving from a passive hardware fix to a low-fidelity automated prototype.

Design Alpha: The Hardware Governor (Passive Limiter)

This is the most rudimentary, plug-and-play design. It requires no code and no network infrastructure. It physically prevents the audio signal from exceeding a comfortable decibel limit, neutralizing the commercial's volume spike instantly.

Design Beta: The Automated IR Protocol (Active Monitoring)

Should a more programmable, localized solution be desired without altering the primary audio chain, one can employ a microcontroller to act as an automated sentry. This leverages basic hardware scavenging and scripting to physically mute the television.

The Process Flow:

An elegant deduction, sir. You have precisely described the concept of audio fingerprinting, which is the exact algorithmic foundation utilized by music recognition services such as Shazam.

Transitioning from a simple volume threshold to pattern recognition elevates the system from a brute-force tool to an intelligent, precise filter. It ensures the system never accidentally mutes a loud action sequence in a film, as it is searching for a highly specific digital signature.

Here is the engineering breakdown of how this sound profiling is executed.

The Mechanics of Audio Fingerprinting

To compress an advertisement into a recognizable pattern, the raw audio must be mathematically transformed.

  • The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT): The microcontroller captures the audio signal in the time domain (amplitude over time). An FFT algorithm converts this data into the frequency domain, revealing which specific frequencies (pitches) are present and their relative strengths at any given millisecond. The computational complexity of this transformation is $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$.
  • Spectrogram Generation: This frequency data creates a rolling 3D map of the audio, plotting time against frequency and amplitude.
  • Constellation Mapping: The algorithm scans the spectrogram and identifies the points of highest energy—the "anchor peaks." By mapping the relationship between these peaks (e.g., Frequency A occurs exactly 45 milliseconds before Frequency B), it creates a constellation map that is highly resistant to background noise or volume changes.
  • Hashing: These peak relationships are converted into a compact alphanumeric hash. This is the "fingerprint" of the commercial.

Hardware Architecture: The Distributed Approach

While the Raspberry Pi Pico W is highly capable, performing continuous FFT calculations and storing an ever-expanding database of commercial fingerprints locally would quickly exhaust its 264KB of RAM.

2. The Network Stream Instead of processing the audio locally, the Pico streams this lightweight data buffer over the local Wi-Fi network via WebSockets or UDP.

3. The Brain (Centralized Server) A script running on a more powerful centralized machine receives the stream. This server performs the FFT, extracts the constellation hashes, and compares them against a local SQLite database of known advertisements.

4. The Execution Command The moment the server confirms a hash match (e.g., a match for the specific frequency pattern of a heavily rotated insurance commercial), it transmits a command back to the Pico W. The Pico instantly fires the IR LED, muting the television.

This architecture allows the processing logic and the database of ad fingerprints to be managed within a primary server environment, keeping the physical hardware near the television exceptionally lightweight and discreet.

The concept of taking the integral of the audio to find the "higher level" sections is the correct approach. In signal processing, this is calculated as the continuous Audio Energy, or the Root Mean Square (RMS) over a sliding time window.

Instead of analyzing complex frequencies, the system calculates the area under the curve of the audio waveform:

$$E(t) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T} \int_{t-T}^{t} [x(\tau)]^2 d\tau}$$

By continuously integrating the squared amplitude $x(\tau)$ over a short window $T$, the system creates a lightweight computational tripwire. It ignores the dialogue and only watches for the sustained, elevated area under the curve that characterizes heavily compressed commercial mixing.

Stage 2: Boundary Detection via the Derivative

Finding the exact start of the advertisement requires looking at the rate of change. Broadcast transitions almost always feature a split-second of pure silence (a near-zero amplitude) followed instantly by the commercial's peak volume.

By calculating the derivative of the audio energy with respect to time, the system can pinpoint these boundaries:

$$\frac{dE}{dt}$$

A massive, near-instantaneous positive spike in this derivative mathematically flags the exact boundary of a new broadcast segment. The system now knows exactly where the advertisement begins.

Once the boundary is identified, the system can hone in on the start of the ad, just as hypothesized.

Because the exact starting boundary is mathematically marked, the algorithm does not need to analyze the entire 30-second or 60-second commercial. It only needs to compute the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and hash the first two to three seconds of the audio.

turns.prompt_text: How does FAT32 work? I guess, how do micro SDs SD cards? And I'm sure switch games and Nintendo DS games. How do they all work? Do they all work? Similarly, or are they different?
turns.response_html:
It is a great observation to group these together. On the outside, a MicroSD card, a Nintendo DS game, and a Switch cartridge look like virtually the same thing: tiny squares of plastic with metal pins on the back.

At a fundamental hardware level, they do work similarly—they all use solid-state, non-volatile memory to store data without needing power. However, how they organize that data (the file system) and how they are allowed to be used (read vs. write) makes them very different under the hood.

Here is a breakdown of how the hardware and software of these tiny storage devices function.

1. The Hardware: How SD and MicroSD Cards Work

Inside a MicroSD card is a microscopic grid of memory cells called NAND Flash Memory.

  • Trapping Electrons: The memory cells use something called a "floating gate transistor." When you save a file, a burst of electricity forces electrons through a barrier into a tiny "trap." Once the electrons are trapped there, they stay there even when the power is turned off.
  • Reading the Data: When the device wants to read the data, it checks to see if electrons are in the trap. If they are, it reads a "0." If the trap is empty, it reads a "1." Millions of these 0s and 1s make up your files.
  • The Controller: SD cards also have a tiny "brain" called a microcontroller. Because flash memory degrades a tiny bit every time you erase and rewrite data, this controller constantly moves files around in the background to ensure all the memory cells wear out evenly (a process called "wear leveling").

2. The Software: How FAT32 Works

If the flash memory is a massive warehouse full of blank boxes (the memory cells), FAT32 is the warehouse manager's ledger.

FAT stands for File Allocation Table. It is a file system originally created by Microsoft decades ago.

  • Clusters: FAT32 divides the entire storage drive into equal-sized chunks called "clusters."
  • The Table: At the very beginning of the drive, there is a literal table (the FAT). When you save a video file, it might take up 50 clusters. The FAT writes down exactly which 50 clusters the video is stored in.
  • Chaining: The data doesn't have to be perfectly sequential. If the warehouse is messy, the video file might be split into cluster #4, then #89, then #402. The FAT creates a "chain" so the computer knows exactly where to jump to read the whole file.

Note: FAT32 is universally readable by almost every device (Windows, Mac, Linux, cameras, 3D printers), but it has a hard limit: it cannot store a single file larger than 4GB. This is why modern devices often format large SD cards to "exFAT," which removes this limit.

3. The Proprietary Tech: DS and Switch Cartridges

While Nintendo cartridges use the same fundamental concept of trapping electrons, they are built with different priorities. An SD card is built to be written over and over again; a game cartridge is built to be read incredibly fast and to be highly secure against piracy.

  • Mask ROM vs. Flash: Older cartridges (and some DS games) used Mask ROM (Read-Only Memory). The 0s and 1s were literally physically etched into the silicon at the factory. You could not overwrite them even if you tried. Modern Switch cartridges use a custom, proprietary type of flash memory manufactured by a company called Macronix (called XtraROM).
  • Read Speed over Write Speed: Switch cartridges are designed to stream massive textures and audio files to the console instantly. Their hardware is heavily optimized for reading data, ignoring the complex "wear leveling" controllers found in SD cards.
  • Save Data Evolution: * Nintendo DS: These cartridges had two chips inside. One was the Read-Only game file, and the other was a tiny, separate rewritable flash chip specifically to hold your save data.
    • Nintendo Switch: Switch cartridges do not store save data. They are entirely read-only. All of your save files are stored on the Switch console's internal memory.
